Leaves Turning Yellow Even After Fertilizer: Causes and Fixes
Home / Guides / Why leaves turn yellow even after you apply...
Why leaves turn yellow even after you apply fertilizer, and how to find the real cause

Another bag of urea is the most common answer to yellow leaves, and often the wrong one. If the roots are drowning, or the soil is locking iron, the crop stays yellow while you pay for fertilizer it cannot use.

If leaves stay yellow after fertilizer, the crop is usually not short of that fertilizer. Either the roots cannot take it up (waterlogging, dry soil, root disease, salt, high pH), or the shortage is a different nutrient such as magnesium, sulphur, iron or zinc. Which leaves turn yellow first tells you where to look.
Step 1: which leaves are yellow?
Likely shortage
Old, lower leaves, whole leaf pale
Common after heavy rain or waterlogging, which washes away or locks nitrogen
Old leaves, yellow between green veins
Often on sandy soils, or where much potash is used
Old leaves, yellow or burnt edges
Potash
Edges dry first, then the whole leaf
Young, top leaves, whole leaf pale
Looks like nitrogen shortage but on new leaves
Young leaves, yellow between green veins
Iron or manganese
Very common on high pH, calcareous soils of Gujarat
Young leaves small, crowded, mottled
Short internodes, small narrow leaves
Patches in the field, plants wilt at midday
Root rot, nematodes, termites or waterlogging; dig a plant
These patterns are a guide. Several shortages can show together, and a leaf or soil test confirms them. See deficiency symptoms with photos.
Step 2: check the roots before the bag
Pull out one yellow plant and one green plant. Compare the roots: white and many is healthy; brown, few, rotten or knotted is a root problem.
Waterlogged soil for even two or three days suffocates roots. Fertilizer cannot help until the soil drains.
Very dry soil also stops uptake. Fertilizer on dry soil sits unused.
Salty water or soil makes leaves yellow and burnt at the edges; see salty borewell water.
Cold nights in winter can make leaves pale for a while; they recover as days warm.
Step 3: is the soil locking nutrients?
On soils with pH above about 8, iron, zinc and manganese are present but locked. Adding more to the soil often fails; foliar sprays or chelated forms work better.
Too much phosphorus can lock zinc. Too much potash can lock magnesium.
Low organic matter means nutrients wash away or get locked quickly. See compost and humic acid.
Fix drainage or irrigation first, if roots are the problem.
Get a soil test, and a leaf test if you can, before adding more NPK.
Correct the specific shortage the pattern and test show, at the label dose.
Keep roots strong with organic matter; a healthy root system takes up more of what is already there.
Ask us with a photo of the whole plant, a close-up of the leaf, and the roots.
ICAR-Indian Institute of Soil Science
Why are leaves yellow even after applying urea?
The crop may not be short of nitrogen. Waterlogging, dry soil, root damage, salt, high pH or a shortage of magnesium, sulphur, iron or zinc can all cause yellowing that urea does not fix.
Which deficiency causes yellow leaves between green veins?
On old leaves, usually magnesium. On young leaves, usually iron or manganese, common on high pH soils.
Can too much water make leaves yellow?
Yes. Waterlogged roots cannot breathe or take up nutrients, so leaves turn yellow even with plenty of fertilizer.
Should I spray or add more fertilizer to the soil?
Find the cause first. Locked micronutrients on high pH soil respond better to foliar sprays; root and water problems need fixing before any fertilizer works.
Why Flowers Drop Before Fruit Set, and What Helps
Home / Guides / Why flowers drop before fruit set in...
Why flowers drop before fruit set in vegetables, cotton and fruit crops, and what helps

A field full of flowers is not a field full of fruit. Heat, thirst, too much urea or a few thrips inside the flowers can empty the plant in a week, and the spray most farmers reach for fixes none of them.

Every crop sheds some flowers; that is normal. Heavy flower drop is usually caused by heat or cold, a dry or waterlogged root zone, too much nitrogen, sucking pests such as thrips and mites, poor pollination, or a shortage of boron. Find which one applies before you spray anything.
Normal drop and problem drop

A plant makes more flowers than it can carry. Cotton sheds many of its squares and young bolls, and a mango panicle keeps only a few fruits out of hundreds of flowers. It becomes a problem when the drop is sudden, most flowers fall, or the plant keeps flowering and setting nothing.
The common causes
What happens
What helps
Very hot days and hot winds dry pollen; tomato and chilli drop flowers in heat waves
Irrigate in the evening, mulch, use shade nets in nurseries
Cold and fog
Pollen does not work well on cold nights; mango and vegetables set poorly in long foggy spells
Wait for warmer days; protect flowers from mildew
Water stress
Dry spells, or a sudden flood after a dry spell
Light, regular irrigation; drip where possible
Too much nitrogen
The plant grows leaves instead of holding flowers
Cut nitrogen at flowering; balance with potash
Thrips, mites, hoppers
They feed on flower parts and buds
Check the inside of flowers with a white paper; act early
Poor pollination
Few bees and insects, often after sprays at bloom
Do not spray open flowers; spray morning or evening
Boron shortage
Pollen tubes do not grow; flowers fall or fruit is misshapen
Correct only if a soil or leaf test, or clear symptoms, show it
Crop notes
Tomato, chilli, brinjal: heat, thrips and mites, and too much nitrogen are the usual causes. See chilli and vegetables.
Cotton: squares and young bolls fall with water stress, cloudy wet spells, excess nitrogen and sucking pests. See cotton.
Pomegranate: male flowers always fall; that is normal. Watch for heat and irregular water. See pomegranate.
Mango: see mango flower and fruit drop and mango flowering care.
Before you spray
Look at the dropped flowers: a clean break with no damage points to stress; brown, chewed or scarred flowers point to pests or disease.
Check soil moisture with your hand at root depth.
Think back over the last week: heat wave, cold spell, heavy rain, a big urea dose or a spray at bloom?
Growth regulators are sold for flower drop. Use them only on your state university's or KVK's advice, at the label dose.

Seaweed and amino acid based products are used before and during flowering to help plants cope with heat and cold stress. They support a crop that is watered and fed well; they do not fix a pest or water problem. See what biostimulants are and boron.
ICAR-National Centre for Integrated Pest Management
Why are my flowers dropping before fruit set?
Usually heat or cold, water stress, too much nitrogen, sucking pests like thrips and mites, poor pollination or boron shortage. Some flower drop is normal in every crop.
Why do tomato and chilli flowers fall?
Most often heat waves and hot winds, thrips and mites, irregular water or too much nitrogen.
Does boron stop flower drop?
Only where boron is short. Boron helps pollen grow and fruit set. Adding it where it is not short does not help, and too much is harmful.
Should I spray a hormone to stop flower drop?
Only on your state university's or KVK's advice, at the label dose, after you have ruled out water, heat and pests.
Hard, Compact Soil: Why It Happens and How to Fix It
Home / Guides / Why soil becomes hard, compact and less...
Why soil becomes hard, compact and less productive, and how to bring it back

Your crop's roots may be stopping at the same depth your plough stops. Below that line sits a hard layer that no fertilizer can soften, and every season of ploughing at the same depth makes it harder.

Soil turns hard when organic matter falls, when it is ploughed or driven on while wet, when the same depth is tilled every year (a plough pan), or when sodium builds up from irrigation water. Roots then stay shallow, water runs off or stands, and yields fall. Organic matter, the right tillage at the right moisture, and gypsum where sodium is the cause bring it back.
Why soil becomes hard
Organic matter has fallen. Organic matter is the glue that keeps soil crumbly.
Ploughing or running a tractor on wet soil smears and packs it.
Tilling to the same depth every year forms a hard layer, a plough pan, just below.
Bare soil under heavy rain or flood irrigation forms a crust on top.
Sodium from irrigation water makes clay soils sticky when wet and hard as stone when dry.
Check your soil in 10 minutes
Push a steel rod into moist soil. If it stops suddenly at 15 to 25 cm, there is a plough pan.
Dig a pit 45 cm deep. Roots turning sideways at one level show the hard layer.
Drop a dry clod in a glass of water. A healthy clod holds together; a clod that melts into mud has poor structure; cloudy water that does not settle can point to sodium.
Watch after irrigation: water standing for a day, or running off, shows poor infiltration.
A soil test with pH, EC and, where needed, exchangeable sodium confirms a sodic soil. See how to take a soil sample.
How to loosen it
Break a plough pan once with a chisel plough or subsoiler, when the soil is dry enough to crack, not wet.
Then keep it open: grow deep-rooted crops, green manure such as dhaincha or sunhemp, and return crop residues.
Add compost or farmyard manure every season. See compost and humic acid.
Do not plough or drive on wet soil.
Mulch or keep the soil covered, so rain does not crust it.
Use gypsum only where a soil or water test shows sodium is the problem, on a lab's advice.
Why yields fall on old land, soil microbial activity and soil health.
ICAR-Central Soil Salinity Research Institute (sodic soils)
Why is my soil becoming hard?
Usually falling organic matter, ploughing or driving on wet soil, a plough pan from tilling the same depth every year, crusting from heavy rain, or sodium from irrigation water.
How do I know if I have a plough pan?
Push a steel rod into moist soil. If it stops suddenly at about 15 to 25 cm, or roots turn sideways at one level in a pit, there is a hard layer.
Does gypsum soften hard soil?
Only where sodium causes the hardness. On ordinary compact soil, organic matter and correct tillage help; gypsum does not.
How long does it take to improve compact soil?
Breaking a plough pan works at once, but the soil packs again unless organic matter and good practice keep it open. Real improvement takes a few seasons.
How to Improve Soil Microbial Activity and Beneficial Bacteria
Home / Guides / How to improve soil microbial activity
How to improve soil microbial activity: feeding the life that feeds your crop

A handful of healthy soil holds more living organisms than there are people in India. They feed your crop every day, and they go hungry the moment the field is burnt, left bare or starved of organic matter.

Soil microbes need food (organic matter and living roots), water, air and cover. Feed them with compost, crop residues, green manure and living roots in the soil for as much of the year as possible. Avoid burning, bare soil, waterlogging and heavy tillage. Biofertilizers add useful microbes, but they survive only in a soil that feeds them.
What microbes do for your crop
Break down crop residues and manure into nutrients plants can use.
Free phosphorus, potash and zinc locked in the soil.
Fix nitrogen from the air, in legume roots and around other crops.
Make the glue that holds soil in crumbs, so water and roots move freely.
Compete with, and keep down, some disease-causing fungi.
What feeds them
Organic matter: compost, farmyard manure, crop residues. See how to start composting.
Living roots: roots release sugars that feed microbes. Avoid long bare fallows.
Variety: rotations and intercrops feed a wider range of microbes than one crop every year.
Moisture and air together: moist, crumbly soil, not dry dust and not waterlogged mud.
What harms them
Burning residues, which removes their food and heats the surface.
Bare soil in summer sun.
Waterlogging, which drives out air.
Frequent deep tillage, which breaks fungal networks and burns organic matter.
Seed or soil treated with chemicals at the same time as live biofertilizers; apply them separately, as the label says.
Signs of a living soil
Earthworms and their casts after rain.
A sweet, earthy smell when you dig.
Crumbly soil that holds together in a ball but breaks easily.
Crop residues that disappear within a season instead of lying for a year.
Water that soaks in quickly after irrigation.
Where biofertilizers fit

Biofertilizers add specific useful microbes, such as nitrogen fixers or phosphate solubilisers. They work best in soil with organic matter and moisture. See which biofertilizers to use and Immunity Consortia.
How can I increase beneficial bacteria in my soil?
Add compost and crop residues, keep living roots in the soil, rotate crops, avoid burning and waterlogging, and use biofertilizers in soil that has organic matter.
Do chemical fertilizers kill soil microbes?

Balanced fertilizer at normal doses does not kill soil life. Long-term use with no organic matter starves it. Some chemical seed treatments and fungicides can harm live biofertilizers applied at the same time.
How do I know my soil is biologically active?
Earthworms, an earthy smell, crumbly structure, residues that break down within a season, and water that soaks in quickly.
Which Biofertilizers to Use: A Crop-by-Crop Guide
Home / Guides / Which biofertilizers to use for your crop, and...
Which biofertilizers to use for your crop, and how to make them work
A biofertilizer is alive. Leave it in a hot shop or mix it with fungicide-treated seed, and you are paying for a packet of dead microbes.

Choose biofertilizers by the job: Rhizobium for pulses and groundnut, Azotobacter or Azospirillum for cereals, vegetables and cotton, Acetobacter for sugarcane, PSB for phosphorus, KMB for potash, ZSB for zinc, and mycorrhiza for roots. They are living products, so freshness, storage and soil organic matter decide whether they work.
What each one does
Biofertilizer
What it does
Rhizobium
Fixes nitrogen in root nodules
Gram, tur, moong, urad, soybean, groundnut
Azotobacter
Fixes nitrogen around roots
Wheat, cotton, vegetables, many non-legumes
Azospirillum
Fixes nitrogen, supports root growth
Maize, sorghum, millets, paddy
Acetobacter
Fixes nitrogen inside the plant
PSB and PSF
Free locked phosphorus
KMB
Free potash from soil minerals
ZSB
Free locked zinc
All crops, especially on high pH soils
Mycorrhiza
Extends roots to reach water and phosphorus
Fruit trees, vegetables, many field crops
Consortia
Several of the above together
Where one product is easier than many
How to apply them
Seed treatment: coat seed just before sowing and sow within a few hours.
Seedling dip: dip roots of transplants before planting.
Soil: mix with well-rotted compost or farmyard manure and apply in the root zone.
Drip: some liquid products can go through drip; follow the label.
Always at the dose and method on the label.
Why biofertilizers sometimes fail
Old or badly stored product. Keep packs in a cool, shaded place, never in the sun or a hot vehicle, and use before expiry.
Mixed with chemical seed treatment or fungicide at the same time. Apply them separately.
Dry soil. Microbes need moisture to settle in.
Soil with almost no organic matter, where they have nothing to live on.
Wrong match: Rhizobium on a non-legume does nothing.
What to expect

Biofertilizers support nutrient supply and root health over a season, and can let many growers reduce chemical fertilizer. They do not replace all fertilizer at once, and results build over seasons with organic matter. Use products approved under the Fertiliser Control Order. See soil microbial activity and reduce chemical fertilizer without losing yield.
National Centre for Organic and Natural Farming
Which biofertilizer is best?

There is no single best. Choose by crop and job: Rhizobium for pulses, Azotobacter or Azospirillum for cereals and vegetables, Acetobacter for sugarcane, PSB for phosphorus, KMB for potash, ZSB for zinc.
Can biofertilizers replace chemical fertilizers?
Not fully at once. They help the crop get more from soil and fertilizer, so many growers can reduce chemical use step by step.
Can I mix biofertilizer with fungicide seed treatment?
Not at the same time. Apply them separately, as the label says, because fungicides can kill the microbes.
How should biofertilizers be stored?
In a cool, shaded place, away from sun and heat, and used before the expiry date.
How to Reduce Chemical Fertilizer Without Reducing Yield
Home / Guides / How to reduce chemical fertilizer without...
How to reduce chemical fertilizer without losing yield: a step-by-step path
Many farms in Gujarat apply phosphorus every year to soil already rich in it. Cutting chemical fertilizer starts with cutting what the crop never uses, not what it needs.

Cut waste first, not the crop's food. Test the soil to stop applying what is already there, place and split fertilizer so more reaches the roots, build organic matter, and add biofertilizers. Reduce in steps over seasons, comparing a strip of the field each time, rather than stopping all fertilizer at once.
Why cutting all at once fails

A field used to high chemical doses, with low organic matter, cannot feed a crop on its own in one season. Growers who stop suddenly often lose yield and go back. Growers who reduce step by step, while building the soil, usually keep their yield and lower their cost.
The path, step by step
Season 1
Soil test; stop applying nutrients the test shows are high; place fertilizer near roots; split nitrogen
Season 1 onward
Add compost or farmyard manure; return crop residues; add biofertilizers suited to the crop
Season 2
Reduce chemical NPK by a modest share on one test strip; compare yield with the rest of the field
Season 3 onward
If the test strip held its yield, extend the reduction; test the soil again
Where most fertilizer is wasted
Applying phosphorus every year on soils already high in it.
Broadcasting on the surface instead of placing near roots.
Giving all the nitrogen at once, much of it lost before the crop can use it.
Fertilizer on dry soil, or just before heavy rain.
Ignoring zinc, sulphur or boron, so the NPK cannot do its job.
Tools that help
Soil and leaf tests. See how to take a soil sample.
Compost and humic substances. See compost and humic acid.
Biofertilizers. See which biofertilizers to use.
Legumes and green manure in the rotation.
Drip fertigation, which puts small amounts where the roots are.
When DAP is short: what to use instead of DAP.
Soil Health Card, Government of India
How can I reduce chemical fertilizer without losing yield?
Test the soil, stop applying what is already high, place and split fertilizer, build organic matter, add biofertilizers, and reduce in steps on a test strip before the whole field.
Can I stop chemical fertilizer completely?
Stopping suddenly usually lowers yield. Reducing step by step over seasons, while building organic matter, is safer.
How much fertilizer can I save?
It depends on your soil and how much was being wasted. A soil test and a test strip in your own field are the honest way to find out.
Organic Farming vs Natural Farming: What Is the Difference?
Home / Guides / Organic farming vs natural farming
Organic farming vs natural farming: the difference, the rules and which suits you

Organic and natural farming both say no to chemicals, but they are not the same. One can earn a certified price premium; the other aims to cut what you buy. Choosing the wrong one for your market costs years.

Both avoid synthetic chemicals. Organic farming allows bought organic inputs such as compost, manures, biofertilizers and approved products, and can be certified (NPOP for export, PGS-India for the domestic market) after a conversion period. Natural farming relies mainly on on-farm inputs such as cow dung and urine preparations, mulching and mixed cropping, with minimal bought inputs, and is promoted by the government's National Mission on Natural Farming.
Organic farming
Natural farming

Not allowed
Not allowed

Kept to a minimum; mostly made on the farm
Typical inputs
Compost, vermicompost, FYM, biofertilizers, green manure
Jeevamrut, beejamrut, mulch, mixed crops, desi cow based preparations
Certification

Not required; some states support group recognition

No formal period
Market

Mostly local and direct sales
What both share
Building soil organic matter and soil life.
Mulching and keeping soil covered.
Crop rotation, intercropping and legumes.
Biological pest management.
Patience: yields often dip in the first seasons and recover as the soil improves.
If you want to sell certified produce, especially for export, choose organic and plan certification from the start.
If you want to cut input cost and sell locally, natural farming practices can fit.
Many growers start with one plot, not the whole farm, and expand what works.
Either way, keep records of what you apply and what you harvest.

What is the difference between organic and natural farming?
Organic farming allows bought organic inputs and can be certified. Natural farming relies mainly on on-farm preparations and mulching with minimal bought inputs, and usually is not certified.
Is natural farming the same as zero budget natural farming?
Natural farming in India grew out of what was called zero budget natural farming. The government now promotes it under the National Mission on Natural Farming.
How long does organic certification take?
Usually a 2 year conversion period for seasonal crops and 3 years for perennial crops before produce can be sold as certified organic.
Can I use biofertilizers in natural farming?
Natural farming keeps bought inputs to a minimum, but many growers use biofertilizers during the change. In certified organic farming, approved biofertilizers are allowed.
Biological Pest and Disease Control: A Farmer's Guide
Home / Guides / Biological pest and disease control
Biological pest and disease control: what works, and how to use it well
A single Trichogramma card holds thousands of tiny wasps that hunt borer eggs before they hatch. Biological control is not weaker than chemicals; it is earlier.

Biological control uses living organisms and natural products to keep pests and diseases below damaging levels: beneficial fungi and bacteria such as Trichoderma, Pseudomonas, Beauveria and Metarhizium, viruses such as NPV, parasitoids such as Trichogramma, and traps and neem. They work best early and preventively, as part of integrated pest management, not as a last rescue.
The main tools
What it is
Used against
Trichoderma
Soil fungus
Root rot, wilt, damping off; seed and soil treatment
Pseudomonas fluorescens
Bacterium
Several leaf and root diseases; seed, soil and spray
Beauveria bassiana
Insect-killing fungus
Hoppers, whitefly, borers, beetles
Metarhizium anisopliae
Insect-killing fungus
White grub, termites, hoppers
NPV (nuclear polyhedrosis virus)
Virus specific to one pest
Helicoverpa and Spodoptera caterpillars
Trichogramma cards
Tiny wasp that kills pest eggs
Borers in sugarcane, cotton bollworms
Pheromone traps
Lure male moths
Monitoring and mass trapping of bollworms, fruit fly, borers
Yellow and blue sticky traps
Catch flying insects
Whitefly, aphids, thrips
Neem products
Plant extract
Feeding deterrent and growth disruptor for many sucking and chewing pests
Rules that make them work
Start early. Biologicals prevent and slow pests; they rarely rescue a crop that is already badly hit.
Fungal products need humidity; spray in the evening.
Do not mix live fungal or bacterial products with chemical fungicides in the same tank.
Use fresh product from a registered source, stored cool, before expiry. Bio-pesticides must be registered with the Central Insecticides Board.
Count pests with traps and field checks, so you act at the right time.
Protect natural enemies: ladybirds, spiders and lacewings are free pest control. Avoid broad-spectrum sprays where you can.
Prevention first
Healthy seed and seed treatment.
Crop rotation, and removing infected plants and residues.
Balanced nutrition: too much nitrogen invites sucking pests.
Good drainage and spacing so leaves dry quickly.
Strong roots and healthy soil; see soil microbial activity.
When to use chemicals

When pests cross the level that causes economic loss and biological options cannot hold them, a registered chemical at the label dose may be needed. Choose the most specific product, and leave a gap before returning to biologicals. See mango flowering care and potato blight for crop examples.
Central Insecticides Board and Registration Committee
What is biological pest control?
Using living organisms and natural products, such as beneficial fungi, bacteria, viruses, parasitic wasps, traps and neem, to keep pests and diseases below damaging levels.
Does Trichoderma control root rot?
Trichoderma is widely used as a seed and soil treatment to protect roots against root rot, wilt and damping off. It works best as prevention.
Can I mix bio-pesticides with chemical fungicides?
Do not mix live fungal or bacterial products with chemical fungicides in the same tank; the fungicide can kill them.
Do biological controls work as fast as chemicals?
Usually slower. They work best early and as prevention, combined with traps, monitoring and good crop care.
